50426.etyen:
From seil (“sail”) + -maker (“craftsperson-forming suffix”), literally “sail-maker”.
The second element -maker (“craftsperson-forming suffix”) is from Old Norse -makari and Middle Low German -maker. The latter is based on maken (“to make, do”), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *makōn (“to make suitable; prepare; make”), with an occupational suffix from Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz (“occupational agent suffix”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk seglmakar, Danish sejlmager, Swedish segelmakare, Dutch zeilmaker, English sailmaker and Low German Seilmaker (“sailmaker”).

en.g: An inflectional suffix forming the simple past of many class-1 weak verbs, often as an alternative to -a

1000442.etyen: Inherited from Danish -et (“past-participle ending”). The use of the ending in the simple past of weak verbs developed under the influence of native Norwegian dialects, in which the past-tense and participial forms had become identical.

en.g: a parish of Ringsaker, Innlandet, Norway, also used for the surrounding district and former municipality
a former municipality of Buskerud, Norway, renamed Nesbyen in 2020
a surname from habitational, from Norwegian farm names and places named Nes

1000698.etyen:
From the common noun nes (“headland, point of land”), from Old Norse nes (“headland, promontory”), from Proto-Germanic *nasją (“headland, cape”), itself derived from Proto-Germanic *nasō (“nose”), from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s (“nose”). The place names refer to land projecting into water; the Akershus municipality is named from a former parsonage on the headland where Vorma and Glomma meet.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Nes, Danish Næs, Swedish Näs, Icelandic Nes and English Ness (“place-name element”).

a surname originating as a patronymic, originally meaning “son of Mons”

1003002.etyen:
From Mons (“male given name”) + -sen (“patronymic suffix meaning “son of””), with simplification of adjacent ⟨ss⟩ to ⟨s⟩, originally a patronymic meaning “son of Mons”. The given name Mons is a traditional Norwegian form of Magnus.
Compare Danish Monsen and Swedish Månsson (“patronymic surname”).

1004026.etyen: abstinere + -ing, first part verbal noun form of abstinere (“abstain”), from Latin abstinēre, present participle of abstineō (“to withhold”), from both ab- (“from, away from, off”), ab (“from, away from, on, in”), from Proto-Italic *ab, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epó (“off, away”) + and from teneō (“to hold, have, grasp”), from Proto-Italic *tenēō (“to hold”), from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch, extend”). Last part from Old Norse -ingr m, -ingi m, -ing f, from Proto-Germanic *-ingō, *-ungō.

en.g: Nazi-; used as the first element in compounds concerning Nazism or Nazis

1004282.etyen:
Clipping of nazistisk (“Nazi, National Socialist”), used as the first element in compounds. Compare the noun and adjective nazi (“Nazi”).
Compare Danish nazi- and Swedish nazi- (“Nazi-”).

en.g: coco-de-mer; a tall, single-stemmed palm with fan-shaped leaves, Lodoicea maldivica, endemic to the islands of Praslin and Curieuse in the Seychelles and known for producing the largest seeds in the plant kingdom

1004794.etyen:
From the bound stem seychell-, derived from Seychellene (“Seychelles”), + palme (“palm tree”), literally “Seychelles palm”.
Compare the parallel formations Swedish seychellpalm and German Seychellenpalme (“Seychelles palm”).

en.g: baaing, bleating; the act or sound of making the cry represented by bæ, especially of a sheep or goat, or by extension the wailing of an infant
x: Bæinga fra sauene kunne høres over hele jordet.
The bleating of the sheep could be heard across the whole field.

1005050.etyen:
From bæe (“to baa; to bleat; to wail”) + -ing (“action-forming noun suffix”), with loss of the infinitive ending -e (“infinitive ending”) before the suffix.
Ultimately derived from the imitative bæ (“baa”).
